findings.title: Open question: When is a dead runner's lock actually stale?
findings.body: Lines 141-150 run the production build under a runner-owned lock and allow reclaim once the owner process is dead. That assumes owner death means all output writers stopped. If the runner dies while its WXT/build child survives, that child can keep writing `.output/chrome-mv3`; the next runner can reclaim the lock, delete the directory, and build or consume concurrently, recreating mixed-artifact or false-green results. The fixture at line 301 only requires recovery of a dead process's lock, not proof that surviving descendants have stopped.
findings.recommendation: Define lock ownership over the complete process group and reclaim only after all descendant writers are terminated and drained, or use run-unique output directories. Add a fixture that kills the runner mid-build while its child continues writing and proves another run cannot overlap or consume mixed output.

findings.title: Browser parity cannot see browser use through the mandated child-process seam
findings.body: D12 classifies a test as browser-backed by whether it imports Playwright. However, lines 272-274 require gate tests to spawn the executable as a child process, so an overflow-gate test can import only Vitest and `child_process` while the spawned gate imports and launches Playwright. If that test is accidentally named `*.test.mjs`, the parity check sees no Playwright import, accepts it into `bun run test`, and browserless CI attempts to launch Chromium. The fixtures at line 315 cover direct imports and glob membership, not this required transitive execution path.
findings.recommendation: Derive runtime classification from explicit gate/test metadata or inspect the spawned target's dependency/execution path. Add a misnamed test that spawns a Playwright-using gate without importing Playwright itself and require parity to fail.

next_steps: Close stale-lock recovery over surviving child processes or adopt run-unique build outputs.
